summary: Abstract: Efficient sensing remains critical in low-cost Internet of Things (IoT) and Web of Things (WoT)-enabled edge nodes, even when the sensor itself is inexpensive and widely used. The DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor employs a single-wire dig-ital protocol and relies on Arduino libraries for data acquisition, timeout handling, and scheduling behavior. In this paper, eight Arduino DHT11 libraries are benchmarked on an Arduino Uno R3 using six criteria: flash memory usage, SRAM consumption, average measured call duration, timing variability, maximum CPU blocking time, and failure-recovery behavior. The results reveal substantial performance trade-offs. Aver-age measured call durations ranged from 5,588 µs for the asynchronous DHT Sensors Non-Blocking implementation to approximately 1.04 s for DHT11; however, these measurements reflect different execution semantics and should not be interpreted as directly equivalent end-to-end acquisition latencies. Flash usage ranged from 4,288 to 5,244 bytes, while SRAM consumption ranged from 238 to 266 bytes. TroykaDHT and SDHT delivered the most stable low-latency readings, DFRobot_DHT11 minimized SRAM usage, and DHT Sensors Non-Blocking was most suitable when asynchronous execution and reduced continuous CPU occupation were required. This study does not directly benchmark application-layer protocols or cloud services, such as HTTP, MQTT, REST, or WebSocket; instead, it characterizes sensing-layer behavior that can influence data freshness, task scheduling, and overall responsiveness in resource-constrained IoT/WoT edge deployments.
title: Performance Analysis of Arduino DHT11 Sensor Libraries for Resource-constrained IoT/WoT Edge Nodes.

summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.

summary: The laws of physics are CPT-symmetric, yet laboratory quantum mechanics prepares the past and only samples the future. This working paper distinguishes five levels of taking the symmetry seriously — symmetric laws with the open future left implicit, a two-boundary description, symmetric processes, a nontrivial final boundary, and laboratory access to it — places published views and experiments on them, and states what each predicts for a final-boundary test, in which an engineered terminal acts on a flag and an entangled partner is read on every trial. Exact results: an open future propagates backward through any physical channel; a terminal can only transfer, never manufacture, final-side contrast, giving lambda = tanh(hbar omega / 2 k T_f) in a swap model, the mirror of a reset; a clamp of budget A needs an energy of at least k T_f ln A in some branch; under free local control any every-trial final condition signals, with visibility equal to the clamp strength. Under stated transfer models a null reads as a lower bound on a swap-equivalent final temperature (Partridge: above 3.5e7 K for escaping microwaves; planned qubit tests: about 27 K and 360 K). The paper audits transport to the future, specifies what any physical source of a final condition must supply, and finds that no named candidate meets the specification. CPT motivates the reversed-resource question; channel duality bounds its possible transfer; laboratory access remains an additional physical hypothesis, decided only by experiment. No new experimental result is reported. Drafted with AI assistance and revised after AI-assisted reviews; responsibility rests with the author.

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23121305 . This narrative review asks how psychosexual rehabilitation after cancer can be delivered at scale, rather than describing how common sexual dysfunction is. The author organizes the intervention evidence by intensity of care. Low-intensity measures (structured discussion, lubricants and moisturizers, topical lidocaine, brief clinician training) are cheap and reasonably supported. Two widely recommended physical interventions have weaker evidence than assumed: scheduled PDE5 inhibitor "penile rehabilitation" and routine vaginal dilation during radiotherapy. Psychological interventions show small pooled effects, but moderate effects in targeted trials, most clearly therapist-guided internet-based CBT in breast cancer. From this the author proposes a five-step stepped-care model (Steps 0–4, built on extended PLISSIT) with explicit criteria for stepping up and down, plus adaptations for AYA, men on ADT, and sexual and gender minority survivors. The paper moves the field forward by reframing the problem as one of delivery, by challenging two entrenched practices, and by turning scattered evidence into a model that oncology teams, including nurses, could adopt and test. Major issues Methods are not reproducible. The review relies on "targeted searches" with no databases, dates, search terms, or selection process described. Evidence is "appraised qualitatively" with no tool such as GRADE or risk-of-bias assessment. Claims like "strongest trial evidence in breast cancer" may reflect selective sampling. The stepped-care model is not empirically validated. It was derived by the author "mapping" interventions to levels of care, with no consensus process, stakeholder input, or implementation data. The 8–12 week step-up threshold has no cited support. The conclusion that evidence "supports matching intensity to need" goes beyond what the cited studies tested, since none compared stepped care with usual care or direct referral (the paper admits this only at the end). Evidence for Steps 0–2 is mostly clinician-level, not patient-level. The cited training studies show clinicians discuss sexuality more often, not that patient outcomes improve. Yet these steps form the base of the model. Feasibility of nurse- or clinician-delivered care also rests largely on one HSCT trial. Key claims rest on weak or non-peer-reviewed sources. The HSCT multimodal trial [34] is a conference abstract that is called "important for the model." Other supports [28, 47] are also abstracts. Pilot RCTs (23 and 29 couples) underpin the "medium-to-large" couple therapy claims. The paper applies evidence standards inconsistently. It criticizes penile rehabilitation and during-radiotherapy dilation for weak evidence, then recommends supported dilation after radiotherapy based on observational data and an uncontrolled 53-woman cohort (11.5% to 60.9% pre-post), and cites a regimen from an abstract [28]. Inference from pooled versus targeted effects is speculative. The difference (SMD 0.24 vs. d 0.43–0.72) is taken to show that interventions work best when targeted, which supports stepped care. It could equally reflect heterogeneity, study quality, outcome measures, or small-study effects. Effect sizes of different metrics are also compared without confidence intervals. There is no limitations section. It should cover search bias, the breast-cancer skew, scarce data for men, SGM, and LMIC settings, and the lack of cost and workforce evidence. Minor issues PLISSIT is never spelled out, and AYA HOPE is not defined. "Psychosexual rehabilitation" is defined as a staged process but used loosely to include medical and physical treatments. A tighter definition would help. Table 2 level-of-care labels are confusing ("Steps 0–2", "Step 2 (on-demand use)" for a scheduled intervention). The HSCT row gives no sample size. summary: Replication package for the article The five determinants of productivity growth do not form a system: a joint test with 80 economies, 2000-2019 . The growth of productivity is often attributed to five determinants presented as a system: trade openness, macroeconomic stability and institutions as conditions, and creative destruction and R&D capacity as channels. The package tests this system with public data for 80 economies in four five-year windows of 2000-2019 (254 country-windows), with a partial least squares path model and with equivalence tests (two one-sided tests), and it examines convergence in total factor productivity for 119 countries with three measures of the distance to the frontier. Contents. Python code ( codigo/ ): construction of the country-window panel, own implementation of PLS path modelling with cluster bootstrap, the two path models, a ladder of 24 variants, equivalence tests, convergence regressions by window, dispersion of TFP levels by year, a placebo for the estimates with country effects, out-of-sample prediction and the figures; an R script that estimates the path models again with seminr; the raw files as downloaded on 1 October 2026 with their sources ( datos/raw/FUENTES.md ); processed data; every table and figure ( salidas/ ); and the 73 numbers of the manuscript recomputed by an independent route ( cifras_reportadas.csv ). Reproduction. cd codigo; python ejecutar_todo.py runs without an internet connection in about 25 minutes (Python 3 with pandas, numpy, scipy, statsmodels, linearmodels and matplotlib). Sources. Penn World Table 11.0 (Groningen Growth and Development Centre, doi:10.34894/FABVLR, CC BY 4.0); World Development Indicators and Worldwide Governance Indicators (World Bank, CC BY 4.0); Fiscal Monitor and World Economic Outlook databases (International Monetary Fund). Variable and file names are in Spanish; the README has a glossary.

summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

summary: Dependency parsers often receive morphological features as part of their input, but the source and completeness of those features are rarely treated as experimental variables. We study German Case in a controlled setting by comparing dependency parsers trained with no Case, independently predicted Case, and gold Case. Using pinned German-GSD and German-HDT Universal Dependencies resources, we audit Case coverage and provenance, construct matched feature conditions, and evaluate both in-domain parsing and cross-treebank transfer. In a three-seed, 1,000-step T4 pilot, predicted Case has higher mean labeled attachment than no Case and higher overall mean LAS than gold Case under HDT transfer for all three seeds. The difference is concentrated on tokens where gold Case is missing; on gold-Case-present tokens, predicted Case is 0.47 LAS points below gold Case on average. Sentence-level paired bootstrap intervals for the aggregate HDT comparison exclude zero, while the in-domain predicted-versus-gold comparison remains seed-sensitive. We use these results to study feature source and annotation completeness while treating the parser and training setup as a controlled feasibility study.
title: Feature Source and Annotation Completeness in German Dependency Parsing

Using pinned German-GSD and German-HDT Universal Dependencies resources, we audit Case coverage and provenance, construct matched feature conditions, and evaluate both in-domain parsing and cross-treebank transfer. In a three-seed, 1,000-step T4 pilot, predicted Case has higher mean labeled attachment than no Case and higher overall mean LAS than gold Case under HDT transfer for all three seeds. The difference is concentrated on tokens where gold Case is missing; on gold-Case-present tokens, predicted Case is 0.47 LAS points below gold Case on average. Sentence-level paired bootstrap intervals for the aggregate HDT comparison exclude zero, while the in-domain predicted-versus-gold comparison remains seed-sensitive. We use these results to study feature source and annotation completeness while treating the parser and training setup as a controlled feasibility study.
title: Feature Source and Annotation Completeness in German Dependency Parsing

summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).
title: Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB)

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23121305 . This narrative review asks how psychosexual rehabilitation after cancer can be delivered at scale, rather than describing how common sexual dysfunction is. The author organizes the intervention evidence by intensity of care. Low-intensity measures (structured discussion, lubricants and moisturizers, topical lidocaine, brief clinician training) are cheap and reasonably supported. Two widely recommended physical interventions have weaker evidence than assumed: scheduled PDE5 inhibitor "penile rehabilitation" and routine vaginal dilation during radiotherapy. Psychological interventions show small pooled effects, but moderate effects in targeted trials, most clearly therapist-guided internet-based CBT in breast cancer. From this the author proposes a five-step stepped-care model (Steps 0–4, built on extended PLISSIT) with explicit criteria for stepping up and down, plus adaptations for AYA, men on ADT, and sexual and gender minority survivors. The paper moves the field forward by reframing the problem as one of delivery, by challenging two entrenched practices, and by turning scattered evidence into a model that oncology teams, including nurses, could adopt and test. Major issues Methods are not reproducible. The review relies on "targeted searches" with no databases, dates, search terms, or selection process described. Evidence is "appraised qualitatively" with no tool such as GRADE or risk-of-bias assessment. Claims like "strongest trial evidence in breast cancer" may reflect selective sampling. The stepped-care model is not empirically validated. It was derived by the author "mapping" interventions to levels of care, with no consensus process, stakeholder input, or implementation data. The 8–12 week step-up threshold has no cited support. The conclusion that evidence "supports matching intensity to need" goes beyond what the cited studies tested, since none compared stepped care with usual care or direct referral (the paper admits this only at the end). Evidence for Steps 0–2 is mostly clinician-level, not patient-level. The cited training studies show clinicians discuss sexuality more often, not that patient outcomes improve. Yet these steps form the base of the model. Feasibility of nurse- or clinician-delivered care also rests largely on one HSCT trial. Key claims rest on weak or non-peer-reviewed sources. The HSCT multimodal trial [34] is a conference abstract that is called "important for the model." Other supports [28, 47] are also abstracts. Pilot RCTs (23 and 29 couples) underpin the "medium-to-large" couple therapy claims. The paper applies evidence standards inconsistently. It criticizes penile rehabilitation and during-radiotherapy dilation for weak evidence, then recommends supported dilation after radiotherapy based on observational data and an uncontrolled 53-woman cohort (11.5% to 60.9% pre-post), and cites a regimen from an abstract [28]. Inference from pooled versus targeted effects is speculative. The difference (SMD 0.24 vs. d 0.43–0.72) is taken to show that interventions work best when targeted, which supports stepped care. It could equally reflect heterogeneity, study quality, outcome measures, or small-study effects. Effect sizes of different metrics are also compared without confidence intervals. There is no limitations section. It should cover search bias, the breast-cancer skew, scarce data for men, SGM, and LMIC settings, and the lack of cost and workforce evidence. Minor issues PLISSIT is never spelled out, and AYA HOPE is not defined. "Psychosexual rehabilitation" is defined as a staged process but used loosely to include medical and physical treatments. A tighter definition would help. Table 2 level-of-care labels are confusing ("Steps 0–2", "Step 2 (on-demand use)" for a scheduled intervention). The HSCT row gives no sample size. Table 2 says the CBT
title: PREreview of "Psychosexual Rehabilitation After Cancer: A Narrative Review of the Intervention Evidence and a Stepped-Care Model for Survivorship Practice"

summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

summary: Supplementary benchmark and experiment code for AutoGobra: Automated Specification and Proof Synthesis for Go. The benchmark contains 349 go-gobra-bench tasks with problem programs, reference solutions, required context, task descriptions, verification configuration, feature labels, and source attribution. The code contains the AutoGobra and Direct/OpenCode experiment implementations, operator prompts, runtime routing configuration, dependency declarations, example configurations, and helper scripts. The archives contain no README files, derivation or curation records, answer-removal metadata, review-status fields, feature evidence, progress records, packaging reports, experiment results, or runtime logs. Required problem dependencies are declared under verification and read directly by the experiment code. Private endpoints and credentials are not included. Configure your own service before running experiments.
title: AutoGobra: Automated Specification and Proof Synthesis for Go — Benchmark and Experiment Code

summary: Code, protocol, and aggregate results for the article When Low Response Does Not Mean No Effect: A Methodological Audit of Response-Derived Weak Supervision for Financial News Kittikorn Takham, Thanayut Changruenngam, Tanaphong Prommai, and Aree Binprathan. FinTech (MDPI), submitted. This release is the version of the repository that accompanies the submitted manuscript. Contents Analysis code ( scripts/ ), unit tests ( tests/ ), and settings ( config.json ) The external-replication protocol, its freeze record, the pre-freeze inspection output, and the deviation log ( research/ ) Every aggregate table and figure behind the article and its supplementary materials ( results/ , figures/ ) Byte-identical originals of the hash-locked files ( archive/ ) Check it without any data python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python tools/verify_release.py python -m unittest discover -s tests verify_release.py checks every file against SHA256SUMS , the replication lock, the provenance snapshots, the code behind each result folder, and the equivalence of the released tables with the original run. Not included Thai news text, price panels, and FNSPID are not redistributed. FNSPID can be downloaded from its authors' repository; the README explains how to regenerate the replication from it. Code released under the MIT License.

Extract-only runs defer unavailable vision instead of running the OCR panel pass that later vision replaces; explicit OCR and standalone fallback remain supported (#341). Separate captions beside an ordinary image no longer establish shared-plate ownership when a following image competes (#336). Rejected caption evidence remains inspectable; explicit plates, jointly captioned groups and structural caption links remain supported. Empty and singleton list encodings are accepted; transport failures and malformed/error payloads still fail validation. Gold fidelity scoring attributes cross-page Docling text to its recorded provenance spans, so a stray character on one page cannot make the next page look empty. Species enumeration supports optional limit / offset and continuation in MCP _meta.pagination , preserving existing list fields (#338). Results have a 256 KiB serialized budget. Compatibility restriction: oversized calls without a limit now return pagination_required ; clients enumerating large clades must follow the returned pagination metadata. Small unpaged calls remain complete. See species-list pagination . Scientific text recovery retains source evidence for signs, units, exponents, Chinese encoding and overlapping accent glyphs (#303, #306, #316). Multi-column order, enclosing species treatments, table cells and key branches remain structured through chunking (#304, #307, #308, #319, #334). Uncertain source readings stay visible; extraction policy and OCR producer changes invalidate dependent artifacts. Original damaged-text evidence survives full-page OCR; agreeing regional readings and prepared-word geometry can recover accented tokens without blindly decoding source text (#312). Preparation receipts reach scratch extraction, and stale receipts retire when the producer changes. Treatment headings require explicit taxonomic authority syntax; global sections clear prior species context. Served source provenance uses bounded previews with explicit truncation and evidence counts (#319). Citation surname recovery requires curated author/year evidence and two agreeing unhinted source-crop OCR re

It also makes build decisions and uncertain evidence auditable. Further work on vision crop content and diagnostic/key ranking is tracked below; experimental policies were not added to this release. Fixed Original whitespace lost during full-page OCR can be restored using exact native letters, aligned page anchors and two agreeing source-crop readings; uncertain geometry and structured owners remain explicit (#334). Verified raised source digits also survive OCR that turns them into punctuation (#303). Both producers invalidate preparation and dependent artifacts. Citation groups separated by distant source regions no longer lose author/year context, and uniquely bounded fullwidth markers retain their original source evidence (#317). Recovered caption labels retire stale panel-completion status; inline taxon initials no longer erase explicit panel inventories (#324). Taxonomy scope warnings distinguish replacement, unrestricted snapshots, ancestor inclusion, dry runs and legacy receipts accurately (#298). Concurrent orphan retirement serializes directory and vector cleanup and tolerates an already-moved source without hiding storage errors (#339). Extract-only runs defer unavailable vision instead of running the OCR panel pass that later vision replaces; explicit OCR and standalone fallback remain supported (#341). Separate captions beside an ordinary image no longer establish shared-plate ownership when a following image competes (#336). Rejected caption evidence remains inspectable; explicit plates, jointly captioned groups and structural caption links remain supported. The extraction policy change invalidates dependent materialized figures and chunks. Fully spelled chapter-scoped captions such as Figure 1-2 retain one printed figure identifier and link abbreviated body references to that identity; ordinary plural numerical ranges still expand (#343). Changing the saved figure pixel cap now invalidates extraction and dependent evidence (#344). The SSE smoke test discovers paper, author, taxon and lexicon values from the active bundle (#337). Empty and singleton list encodings are accepted; transport failures and malformed/error payloads still fail validation. Gold fidelity scoring attributes cross-page Docling text to its recorded provenance spans, so a stray character on one page cannot make the next page look empty. Species enumeration supports optional limit / offset and continuation in MCP _meta.pagination , preserving existing list fields (#338). Results have a 256 KiB serialized budget. Compatibility restriction: oversized calls without a limit now return pagination_required ; clients enumerating large clades must follow the returned pagination metadata. Small unpaged calls remain complete. See species-list pagination . Scientific text recovery retains source evidence for signs, units, exponents, Chinese encoding and overlapping accent glyphs (#303, #306, #316). Multi-column order, enclosing species treatments, table cells and key branches remain structured through chunking (#304, #307, #308, #319, #334). Uncertain source readings stay visible; extraction policy and OCR producer changes invalidate dependent artifacts. Original damaged-text evidence survives full-page OCR; agreeing regional readings and prepared-word geometry can recover accented tokens without blindly decoding source text (#312). Preparation receipts reach scratch extraction, and stale receipts retire when the producer changes. Treatment headings require explicit taxonomic authority syntax; global sections clear prior species context. Served source provenance uses bounded previews with explicit truncation and evidence counts (#319). Citation surname recovery requires curated author/year evidence and two agreeing unhinted source-crop OCR re

summary: Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM) describes the photon as an energetic physical entity whose interaction with an external gravitational field proceeds by direct force- and energy–momentum exchange, rather than through the geometric curvature of spacetime. This paper develops the ECM account of photon dynamics in external gravitational fields, with gravitational redshift interpreted as the expenditure of an acquired gravitational interaction-energy component Eɢ rather than as a depletion of the photon’s inherent frequency-defined energy. The photon’s inherent state is fixed by Eᵢₙₕₑᵣₑₙₜ = hf_photon = −Mᵃᵖᵖc², where Mᵃᵖᵖ < 0 is the Negative Apparent Mass (NAM) associated with the energetic reduction of the emitting electron. A coordinate framework for the photon–field interaction is constructed in which successive interaction stages generate external-field momentum displacements through Δpₑₓₜ = h/Δλ and its reverse-branch counterpart Δpₑₓₜ = h/(−Δλ), organised as a symmetric blueshift–redshift trajectory about the inherent reference state. The complete state-generation chain x° → f → Δf → λ → Δλ → Δpₑₓₜ → ΔG is established together with the ECM phase transformation Tₓˆ = x°/360°f = Δt, providing a rigorous, data-driven basis for graphing the exchange without arbitrary coordinates. An explicit nine-point displacement data set is specified, the complete coordinate table is computed, and the exchange trajectory is graphed.
title: Photon Dynamics in External Gravitational Fields: Energy–Momentum Exchange Between Photons and Gravitational Fields in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: Companion archive for the article Accuracy is not reliability: abstention-aware evaluation of large language models on bio-bibliographic claim verification in classical Islamic scholarship (Information Processing & Management, Elsevier, 2026, in press). Contents: the ISNAD benchmark (1,986 scored Turkish claims across five probe types) and the 360-item Turkish/Arabic GAL replication set with gold labels; freeze and exclusion manifests; 64,216 raw model-output records; blank expert-study forms with answer keys; and six analysis scripts with fixed seeds that regenerate the article's tables. summary: The application of machine learning to cryptocurrency price prediction requires a decisive pivot from uncalibrated point forecasting toward structural regime awareness. Standard higher-order central moments fail in cryptocurrency environments because polynomial exponentiation amplifies heavy-tailed noise precisely when stable detection is most critical. The Exact Linear Statistical Moments framework (M1, M2, M3, M4) solves this problem by tracking the true geometric deformation of phase space using robust order statistics. By establishing the Brownian benchmark E[M4] = 2.0, this framework identifies superdiffusive breakdown of restoring forces prior to systemic market crises. When integrated as a dynamic gating engine for multimodal deep learning models (SARIMAX, LSTM, AdaBoost-LSTMs), it resolves the divergence between statistical error metrics and real-world trading solvency, providing an early-warning and capital-preservation pipeline for digital asset markets.
title: Geometric Regime Shift Detection in Cryptocurrency Markets: Enhancing Multimodal Deep Learning with Exact Linear Statistical Moments

summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. Asimismo, incorpora procedimientos para auditoría me

summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. summary: Replication package for an empirical comparison of the retrieval engines an offline, memory-constrained on-device assistant can embed: SQLite/FTS5, DuckDB-FTS, in-memory BM25, an in-memory linear scan, MiniLM with HNSW on CPU, and the on-disk vector store sqlite-vec. Cost (latency, build time, footprint) and retrieval quality are measured together on WikiText-103, SQuAD, Project Gutenberg and the Turkish TQuAD set, with an embedded hybrid and a coverage-gated router, quantized and ONNX encoders, stronger small encoders, an isolated cost decomposition, a downstream answer-recall check, an incremental-update test, bootstrap confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests. The package holds all code, the result files, the published tables and figures, and two checking scripts: one re-derives every table value from the result files, the other redraws the figures and compares them with the published files. The Gutenberg and SQuAD files are included; TQuAD, whose repository has no license, is downloaded and checked against its SHA-256; the WikiText-103 scaling corpus is a separate file in this record. DATA_MANIFEST.txt lists the SHA-256 of every input. The lexical scaling measurement was repeated on one Android phone; everything else was measured on an x86 workstation, and energy was not measured. Code: MIT. Data: their own licenses (public domain for Gutenberg, CC BY-SA for SQuAD and WikiText-103).

summary: This repository gathers two datasets used for the AnDi-J Benchmark web app. Each of them where developed for the respective AnDi Challenge: The Trajectory Analysis Dataset is the challenge phase dataset for tasks 1 and 2 of the 1st AnDi Challenge. The Trajectory Segmentation Dataset is the challenge phase dataset for the Trajectory track (Track 2) of the 2nd AnDi Challenge. This repository is created to facilitate their download from a single source. Please see the AnDi-J documentation, webapp and the respective challenge papers and resources to learn more about these datasets (see below). The datasets only contain input data, no labels, to be used as a pure validation / test dataset.  References: AnDi-J Plugin: https://github.com/gorkamunoz/andi-j 1st AnDi Challenge: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26320-w 2nd AnDi Challenge: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61949-x

summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. When a high-confidence correction is found, GradLint can emit repaired FSL and/or MRtrix gradient files together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs.  The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. This record archives the source code for GradLint v1.1.6, corresponding to the GitHub release published on 2026-10-03. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. Repository: https://github.com/marcotag93/GradLint Release: https://github.com/marcotag93/GradLint/releases/tag/v1.1.6 PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/gradlint/ Concept DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20847595
title: GradLint: Fast gradient-scheme QC, b-vector flip detection, and repair for diffusion MRI

summary: Language functions not only as a means of transmitting information but also as a repository of cultural knowledge, collective experience, and culturally shaped patterns of thought. Consequently, translation involves more than the transfer of lexical and grammatical information between languages. It also requires the interpretation and reconstruction of meanings that are embedded within particular cultural contexts. This issue becomes especially evident in the translation of idioms, proverbs, metaphors, realia, and other culture-specific expressions whose meanings cannot always be derived from their individual lexical components. In Translation Studies, such elements are commonly discussed as culture-specific items (CSIs), which may require particular strategies to preserve their semantic, pragmatic, and cultural dimensions in the target language (Aixelá, 1996).
tags: Idiomatic expressions provide a particularly clear illustration of the relationship between language and culture.
title: AI TRANSLATION OF CULTURE-SPECIFIC AND IDIOMATIC EXPRESSIONS: LINGUISTIC AND CULTURAL CHALLENGES

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23128096 . Summary This paper studies a problem that production ML teams feel but the literature mostly ignores: drift detectors are evaluated on detection accuracy under synthetic, single-shot shifts, while in production they run continuously across many features and time windows — where even small nominal false positive rates accumulate into frequent alerts and, eventually, alarm fatigue. The author simulates a 30-day continuous monitoring cycle on the Adult Income dataset (~30k samples, 14 features) and compares five widely used detectors — PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, and adversarial validation — across batch sizes 50–500 and injected drift magnitudes (5–20 year shifts in the age feature), reporting false-positive days, true positive rate, and time to detection. Headline findings: PSI fires on ~30/30 days below ~200 samples per batch and stabilizes sharply above it; KS achieves the best stability–sensitivity balance (TPR up to 0.90 at the largest shift); MMD shows near-zero sensitivity under default settings; Bonferroni correction suppresses false alarms at the cost of sensitivity. Strengths The framing is the paper's core contribution. Reframing drift detection from a detection-accuracy problem to an operations-reliability problem is exactly the shift practitioners need. I audit ML designs for production readiness, and "the detector works" vs. "the detector is trusted by the on-call team" are different claims — this paper measures the second one. The alarm-fatigue motivation (Sculley et al.) is not decoration; the metric design follows from it. "False positive days out of 30" is a metric an SRE can reason about; it maps directly to pager load. This is a better evaluation currency for monitoring work than AUC-style summaries, and more papers in this space should adopt it. The practical-guidelines table (Table 1) is genuinely useful. The per-detector "practical implication" column — e.g., PSI only above ~200 samples/batch, KS as the reliable default for tabular monitoring — is the kind of artifact that survives the paper and ends up in runbooks. Too many monitoring papers stop at curves; this one tells you what to configure. Experimental transparency is good. Full appendices with detector configurations (binning, thresholds, kernel settings, permutation counts), the monitoring protocol, and complete result tables with mean ± std across 5 seeds. The PSI batch-size table (30.00±0.00 at batch 50 → 0.00±0.00 at batch 500) is striking precisely because the numbers are all visible. Major issues 1. Single dataset, single drift type — generality is the main limitation. Everything rests on Adult Income: tabular, 14 features, and drift injected into one feature (age) as a gradual univariate shift. Real production drift is frequently multivariate, correlated across features, sudden (upstream schema or pipeline changes), or semantic (label drift with stable inputs). The conclusion acknowledges this as future work, but the practical guidelines in Table 1 are written as deployment advice — they should carry an explicit scope warning that the ~200-sample PSI threshold and the KS-default recommendation are calibrated to one tabular dataset, not established as general rules. 2. Label-encoding categoricals before KS/MMD distorts the comparison. Appendix A states categoricals were label-encoded. A two-sample KS test on label-encoded categoricals is not meaningful — the encoding imposes an arbitrary ordinal structure the test then treats as real. MMD with a Gaussian kernel on label-encoded categories has the same problem. This choice may flatter detectors that are insensitive to the distortion and penalize ones that react to it. At minimum, the paper should report a sensitivity analysis with proper categorical handling (e.g., one-hot + appropriate tests, or feature-type-aware detector variants) so readers know wheth
title: PREreview of "When Drift Detectors cry Wolf: False Alarm Rates in continuous ML Monitoring"

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23128096 . Summary This paper studies a problem that production ML teams feel but the literature mostly ignores: drift detectors are evaluated on detection accuracy under synthetic, single-shot shifts, while in production they run continuously across many features and time windows — where even small nominal false positive rates accumulate into frequent alerts and, eventually, alarm fatigue. The author simulates a 30-day continuous monitoring cycle on the Adult Income dataset (~30k samples, 14 features) and compares five widely used detectors — PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, and adversarial validation — across batch sizes 50–500 and injected drift magnitudes (5–20 year shifts in the age feature), reporting false-positive days, true positive rate, and time to detection. Headline findings: PSI fires on ~30/30 days below ~200 samples per batch and stabilizes sharply above it; KS achieves the best stability–sensitivity balance (TPR up to 0.90 at the largest shift); MMD shows near-zero sensitivity under default settings; Bonferroni correction suppresses false alarms at the cost of sensitivity. Strengths The framing is the paper's core contribution. Reframing drift detection from a detection-accuracy problem to an operations-reliability problem is exactly the shift practitioners need. I audit ML designs for production readiness, and "the detector works" vs. "the detector is trusted by the on-call team" are different claims — this paper measures the second one. The alarm-fatigue motivation (Sculley et al.) is not decoration; the metric design follows from it. "False positive days out of 30" is a metric an SRE can reason about; it maps directly to pager load. This is a better evaluation currency for monitoring work than AUC-style summaries, and more papers in this space should adopt it. The practical-guidelines table (Table 1) is genuinely useful. The per-detector "practical implication" column — e.g., PSI only above ~200 samples/batch, KS as the reliable default for tabular monitoring — is the kind of artifact that survives the paper and ends up in runbooks. Too many monitoring papers stop at curves; this one tells you what to configure. Experimental transparency is good. Full appendices with detector configurations (binning, thresholds, kernel settings, permutation counts), the monitoring protocol, and complete result tables with mean ± std across 5 seeds. The PSI batch-size table (30.00±0.00 at batch 50 → 0.00±0.00 at batch 500) is striking precisely because the numbers are all visible. Major issues 1. Single dataset, single drift type — generality is the main limitation. Everything rests on Adult Income: tabular, 14 features, and drift injected into one feature (age) as a gradual univariate shift. Real production drift is frequently multivariate, correlated across features, sudden (upstream schema or pipeline changes), or semantic (label drift with stable inputs). The conclusion acknowledges this as future work, but the practical guidelines in Table 1 are written as deployment advice — they should carry an explicit scope warning that the ~200-sample PSI threshold and the KS-default recommendation are calibrated to one tabular dataset, not established as general rules. 2. Label-encoding categoricals before KS/MMD distorts the comparison. Appendix A states categoricals were label-encoded. A two-sample KS test on label-encoded categoricals is not meaningful — the encoding imposes an arbitrary ordinal structure the test then treats as real. MMD with a Gaussian kernel on label-encoded categories has the same problem. This choice may flatter detectors that are insensitive to the distortion and penalize ones that react to it. At minimum, the paper should report a sensitivity analysis with proper categorical handling (e.g., one-hot + appropriate tests, or feature-type-aware detector variants) so readers know wheth

summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.

summary: Replication package for an empirical comparison of the retrieval engines an offline, memory-constrained on-device assistant can embed: SQLite/FTS5, DuckDB-FTS, in-memory BM25, an in-memory linear scan, MiniLM with HNSW on CPU, and the on-disk vector store sqlite-vec. Cost (latency, build time, footprint) and retrieval quality are measured together on WikiText-103, SQuAD, Project Gutenberg and the Turkish TQuAD set, with an embedded hybrid and a coverage-gated router, quantized and ONNX encoders, stronger small encoders, an isolated cost decomposition, a downstream answer-recall check, an incremental-update test, bootstrap confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests. The package holds all code, the result files, the published tables and figures, and two checking scripts: one re-derives every table value from the result files, the other redraws the figures and compares them with the published files. The SQuAD files and eleven public-domain Project Gutenberg works are included; the copyrighted Metamorphosis translation (Project Gutenberg eBook #5200) and TQuAD, whose repository has no license, are downloaded and checked against their SHA-256; the WikiText-103 scaling corpus is a separate file in this record. DATA_MANIFEST.txt lists the SHA-256 of every input. The lexical scaling measurement was repeated on one Android phone; everything else was measured on an x86 workstation, and energy was not measured. Code: MIT. Data: their own licenses (public domain for the eleven Gutenberg works, CC BY-SA 4.0 for SQuAD, CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL for WikiText-103).

summary: Replication package for an empirical comparison of the retrieval engines an offline, memory-constrained on-device assistant can embed: SQLite/FTS5, DuckDB-FTS, in-memory BM25, an in-memory linear scan, MiniLM with HNSW on CPU, and the on-disk vector store sqlite-vec. Cost (latency, build time, footprint) and retrieval quality are measured together on WikiText-103, SQuAD, Project Gutenberg and the Turkish TQuAD set, with an embedded hybrid and a coverage-gated router, quantized and ONNX encoders, stronger small encoders, an isolated cost decomposition, a downstream answer-recall check, an incremental-update test, bootstrap confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests. The package holds all code, the result files, the published tables and figures, and two checking scripts: one re-derives every table value from the result files, the other redraws the figures and compares them with the published files. The SQuAD files and eleven public-domain Project Gutenberg works are included; the copyrighted Metamorphosis translation (Project Gutenberg eBook #5200) and TQuAD, whose repository has no license, are downloaded and checked against their SHA-256; the WikiText-103 scaling corpus is a separate file in this record. DATA_MANIFEST.txt lists the SHA-256 of every input. The lexical scaling measurement was repeated on one Android phone; everything else was measured on an x86 workstation, and energy was not measured. Code: MIT. Data: their own licenses (public domain for the eleven Gutenberg works, CC BY-SA 4.0 for SQuAD, CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL for WikiText-103).

summary: Anonymised replication package for the paper "Preserving Responsive Specifications Beyond the Source Viewport in Design-to-Code Generation" (FSE 2027 submission). The package contains the 48 frozen responsive specifications of the benchmark, the seven exported generation inputs for every page, and the contracts inferred by Kimi K3 from the desktop metadata. It also holds all 2,016 generated programs from GPT-5.4 mini, Qwen3.5 397B and GLM-4.6V, with two repetitions each. Every program comes with its request, response, render records, element matches and scores. The analysis folder holds the exporter, generation client, renderer, matcher, detector, statistics and R scripts, including the mixed model used in the paper. The package also includes the results, the confirmatory hypothesis and test for the third model, the validation labels and the study logs. README.md inside the archive describes each folder and how to rerun the analysis.
title: Replication package for "Preserving Responsive Specifications Beyond the Source Viewport in Design-to-Code Generation"

summary: This dataset contains the derived summary resources supporting the manuscript Sequence-to-function models prioritize fine-mapped blood eQTLs in African American, Caribbean Hispanic, and Non-Hispanic White participants . The package includes the source tables for every main and supplementary figure and table, model-score summaries, fine-mapping benchmark tables, AUROC resampling summaries, the matched FILER functional-annotation enrichment analysis (inputs, results, and QC), the follow-up analyses that dissect the group difference (score anatomy, resampling, LD, allele frequency, label transfer, within-gene evaluation, annotation baselines), the model-first LD-reduced evaluation (configuration, results, and QC), the eQTLGen replication summary, and row-level prediction tables. The package is split into several archives; the top-level README and MANIFEST describe every file and how the archives fit together. No individual-level genotypes or sample identifiers are included. Analysis code for model scoring, summary analyses, and manuscript figure and table generation is available at https://github.com/Xinyu-Sun/s2f_snp_eqtl_analysis_code, commit b5a9e1270f431a82265d63f0b90ee17eabb9da6c. Version 2026-10-03.

summary: The Riemann workbench now presents completed distinct-zero bounds and all 25 experiment records, with English/Spanish explanations, proof stages, counting scope, source provenance and reproducibility links. Strongest admitted whole-strip distinct-point bound: 30945470743359/36955122080000 = 0.8373797460706156... (EXP-025, attributed external local theorem and reviewed vector-pressure transfer). Separate complete nine-point certificate: 3997934614153/4775507750000 = 0.8371747724947154... (EXP-020). All 96 shards, independent complete-cover audit, 61,029-cell native input comparison, actual-output corruption controls and extracted reproducibility replay pass. Focused companion and two reproducibility archives: Zenodo version 10.5281/zenodo.23128663 . Published bytes remain immutable. A real static Riemann route supports direct access. Recorded evidence is checked before export and again by a fail-closed browser helper. Validation includes 258 selected Riemann tests at the mathematical milestone, 68 export tests, 31 frontend tests, TypeScript/build, repository guards and two complete 20-scenario UI matrices (120 tab visits each; 5,894 full-panel and 1,640 final-bake screenshots, zero failed checks). These are scoped checks, not a full-repository test claim. RH remains open. These bounds count distinct points throughout the critical strip relative to all zeros with multiplicity; they are not a new simple-critical-line proportion. The short-window onset remains 0.534. No effective height, worldwide priority or external peer acceptance is asserted. The external Lean/nanoda local theorem was archived rather than rebuilt locally; native paths share FLINT/Arb. Incomplete EXP-019/023 traversals are excluded from the admitted bound.

summary: Classical metaphysics treats the mutual exclusivity of alternatives as primitive: or, in its physical reading, excludes by nature. This paper argues the polarity should be reversed. Exclusivity is an achievement — stated, interior, structural content of the alternatives them-selves — rather than an intrinsic feature of disjunction; and once exclusion is relocated from the exterior of or to interior content, a new composition regime falls out with no further postulation: the joint regime, in which co-present alternatives simply decline to carry mu-tual negations. The difference between the regimes is fixed by a one-statement test, which answers the suspicion of mere notation; a strict fence separates what the new primitive sup-plies (openness) from anything its occupants might do with it (use), which blocks the two natural misreadings; and the primitive itself receives a deflationary definition: or-jointness is the logic-valued regime of not stating mutual negations on the interior side — obtained by declension, not addition. We argue the proposal reclassifies the color-exclusion problem that fractured the Tractatus, and supplies the determinable-based literature on metaphysical indeterminacy with the composition story it has lacked. A documented fact about the direction of discovery then bears on the proposal’s status: the two composition forms were first extracted, in companion work, from the case-by-case structure of interference phenomena — before the present philosophy existed — so the dichotomy’s shape is explained by what it was extracted from, not by any philosophical purpose it might serve. Whether the world instantiates the joint regime is the companion framework’s proposal, on which no thesis here leans; what the provenance establishes is that the primitive was not gerrymandered for the argument that now exposes it.

summary: This record provides the reproducibility package accompanying the study " Resolving BTEX Mixtures under Infrared Spectral Interference with Dual-Representation Learning." The archive contains frozen author-generated BTEX training, validation, test, and composition-held-out Challenge datasets; final model configurations and random seeds; trained model checkpoints; and source code for spectral simulation, model training and evaluation, representation analysis, Integrated Gradients analysis, hyperparameter optimization, statistical analysis, and external spectral transfer. It also includes audit records for the final hyperparameter-optimization studies and paired-bootstrap analysis, together with provenance information for the external spectral resources used in the study. Raw third-party HITRAN/PNNL, NIST, and U.S. EPA infrared spectra and derived source templates with unconfirmed redistribution rights are not redistributed. Source identifiers, acquisition information, checksums, and preprocessing provenance are provided to support independent retrieval from the original sources.

summary: Code, exact certificate data and Lean 4 formalizations supporting the paper 'Variance and local log-concavity of Poisson-binomial laws' by Brett Reynolds. Computations the proof needs: scripts/verify_pb_compact_monotone.py checks the 32 exact rational inequalities of Section 4.1 using only the Python standard library, and scripts/verify_pb_large_h_range.py checks the expansions for H >= 16 in exact arithmetic (SymPy). scripts/verify_pb_cue_threshold.py certifies the variance threshold in the Haar unitary example with rational bounds on pi. Additional check: a certificate by Bernstein expansions for 3 < H <= 16 (275 positive rational coefficients), with a SymPy generator and an independently written standard-library checker. Formalizations (Lean 4, Mathlib v4.28.0): a proof of Proposition 3.1, and a proof of Theorem 1.1 from the probability-generating polynomial, including the Hillion-Johnson cubic inequalities, strict log-concavity and the maximal-mass bound. Both depend only on Lean's three standard axioms. An earlier conditional formalization is also included. summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . Keywords: Abstract algebra, cyclic groups, direct products, exponent coordinates, re- lation lattices, projection functors, natural transformations, Newton identities, Chinese Remainder Theorem, rank complexity. summary: This dataset supports the study “A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection.” It contains accession-level manifests, derived statistical tables, figure-source data, documentation, software-version information, and analysis code supporting an assembly-first workflow with raw-read reconstruction for publicly available sequencing records. Starting from 44,278 geographically resolved eligible records, 1,687 records had no analyzable public genome input, leaving 42,591 records with an analyzable genome input. Of these, two were excluded during final cohort harmonization, resulting in a final analytical collection of 42,589 K. pneumoniae genomes. This collection comprised 40,093 genomes represented by usable public assemblies and 2,496 genomes reconstructed from publicly available sequencing reads. The deposit does not redistribute genome assemblies or raw sequencing reads. Sequence data should be retrieved from the relevant public repositories using the accession identifiers provided in the manifests. The archived materials support reproduction of the post-assembly cohort audit, statistical summaries, and figures. The exact raw-read preprocessing commands used for the rescued genomes were not retained; consequently, adapter-trimming and quality-filtering parameters are not represented as reproducible components of this deposit. Reconstructed and deposited assemblies were nevertheless evaluated using the same post-assembly quality-control criteria before inclusion in the final analytical collection. Jianhua Li and Jing Guo contributed equally to this work. Jing Chen is the corresponding author. Correspondence: dongqingfei@126.com . Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Xiamen Municipality (No. 3502Z202373092).
