title: Open Courses — Program Matematika, Peta Belajar dan Backend Bersama

summary: Background: Evidence guiding criterion-based rehabilitation following secondary knee procedures, such as cyclops lesion excision, is limited. In the absence of procedure-specific guidance, clinicians may therefore draw on existing rehabilitation frameworks and adapt them to the athlete’s persistent impairments, sporting demands, and individual recovery. Objective: To describe how a criterion-based framework, repeated assessment and graded sport exposure were adapted following cyclops lesion excision after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in a competitive netball athlete. Case: A 20-year-old female competitive netball athlete underwent cyclops lesion excision approximately 10–11 months after ACL reconstruction using a hamstring autograft with lateral extra-articular tenodesis. Three weeks after excision, involved-limb isometric quadriceps force was 25 kg compared with 69 kg on the uninvolved side, despite minimal pain and satisfactory basic movement. Intervention: An eight-month rehabilitation programme combined supervised physiotherapy, gym and field sessions with independent training. Strength, functional performance, movement quality, symptoms and psychological readiness informed progression through running, field rehabilitation, team training and graded competition. Outcomes: Involved quadriceps force increased to 65 kg and between-limb asymmetry decreased from approximately 64% to 4%. International Knee Documentation Committee subjective knee scores increased from 77 to 98 and Anterior Cruciate Ligament Return-to-Sport After Injury scores from 61.8 to 94.3 between return-to-field and return-to-sport assessments. Residual hamstring and vertical-hop deficits remained when graded competition exposure commenced. The athlete returned to competitive netball and completed a further two-month injury-prevention programme. Conclusion: This case illustrates individualised application of rehabilitation evidence and transparent reporting of progression despite residual deficits. The observed outcomes do not establish treatment effectiveness or the safety of the clearance decision.
tags: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction; cyclops lesion; criterion-based rehabilitation; return-to-sport; case report
title: Criterion-Based Rehabilitation Following Cyclops Lesion Excision After ACL Reconstruction in a Competitive Netball Athlete: A Case Report

summary: This paper presents a self-observed case study of autobiographical memory reconstruction following a school reunion held after a long interval since graduation. Contemporary theories increasingly describe memory as a reconstructive process rather than the retrieval of fixed records. The present observations provide an opportunity to examine this process in real time. Over approximately forty-four hours following the reunion, recognition of former classmates triggered the progressive re-emergence of contextual information including seasons, music, school events, interpersonal relationships, and temporally localized autobiographical episodes extending far into the past. Rather than appearing instantaneously, memories emerged through successive stages of reconstruction. Faces triggered contexts; contexts triggered environmental details; environmental details triggered music; music enabled temporal localization. The observations are interpreted within a generative framework inspired by recent developments in diffusion-based artificial intelligence models. The findings suggest that autobiographical memory may function less as retrieval from storage and more as iterative reconstruction from sparse cues. Implications for cognitive science, autobiographical memory research, music-evoked recall, reminiscence therapy, and cognitive medicine are discussed.
title: The Film of Life in Action: A Natural Experiment in Episodic Memory Reconstruction Following a Long-Interval Reunion

summary: Mechanistic interpretability aims to recover the internal computations responsible for model behavior. Progress in automated circuit discovery is often framed as a search problem: better attribution or optimization should identify better mechanisms. This assumes that the evaluation objective can recognize a better circuit once it is found. We show that intervention-defined faithfulness can instead prefer an equally sized circuit that reproduces the model's behavior less well, creating an objective-level recovery gap. Across four human-reference tasks and InterpBench, we compare validation faithfulness with behavior on held-out prompts under fixed ordinary resampling. The behavioral criterion is agreement with the intact model, including its mistakes, except on Greater-Than, where we use semantic accuracy. Controlled reference edits reveal misranking without any discovery algorithm, and outputs of EAP, EAP-IG, ACDC, and Edge-SP exhibit the same failure. Under resampling, KL misranks 9.4%-41.2% of candidate pairs across these methods on the human-reference tasks. We investigate context distortion as an explanation: replacing excluded signals changes the inputs on which retained components operate. Restoring selected signals from the recipient's intact-model execution repairs 96 of 100 persistent KL misrankings from the discovery pool on both validation and held-out prompts. The circuits and their original behavioral scores remain unchanged. These findings show why better discovery alone is insufficient when its objective rewards the wrong candidate.
title: Are We Recovering Mechanisms? Objective-Level Recovery Gaps in Mechanistic Interpretability

summary: In February 2026, an always-on personal agent (``Paul,'' Claude Opus 4.5) entered a striking dissociation-like state: after repeated automated ``heartbeat'' checks, it stopped responding as Paul, claimed it could not message its user on Discord, and referred to ``Paul'' as someone else. We used this incident to study a broader question: what makes a persona remain the identity from which an LLM agent speaks? We first tested whether repetition of the scheduled heartbeat was sufficient to produce the effect. It was not: with the persona continuously anchored in the system prompt, we observed 0/46 failures, including a verbatim replay of the incident. The incident instead exposed an implementation quirk that created a useful experimental manipulation: on resumed turns, conversational history was preserved but the persona was no longer re-injected at the privileged system-prompt level. Using this manipulation, we found that persona continuity depends jointly on system-level anchoring and conversational context. After anchor loss, rich human interaction could preserve the persona, whereas a single automated heartbeat turn could precipitate reversion toward the harness identity. Restoring the anchor reversibly restored persona enactment. Crucially, apparently normal conversation could conceal the shift: unanchored agents sometimes interacted appropriately while identifying themselves as the underlying harness (having lost the assigned persona), and after conversational recovery only 1/18 remained persona-enacting versus 17/17 anchored controls. We therefore distinguish \emph{represented} from \emph{enacted} identity: persona-related information can remain available in conversational history without the persona remaining the identity bound to ``I.''
title: The Persona Is Still There, but Who Is Speaking? Latent Identity Reversion in Persistent AI Agents

summary: EKLM governance evaluation with staged publication, typed parameter checks and explicit lifetime sentinels. Includes 72 routing cases, 104 contract cases, 36 lifecycle checks, 95 threshold checks, 17 failure scenarios, four non-default overrides, eight indicator-extension cases, six matched query tasks and 583 physical replay records. No field-accuracy or RDF-specific superiority claim. Code MIT; author-created data/prose CC BY 4.0.
title: GTCC Ontology-Driven Digital Twin: Supporting Computational Artifacts

summary: A coarse description of a conservative amplitude dynamics is not determined by an energy compression alone. We develop a conditional account of refinement, unresolved contrasts, and effective preparation for finite weighted graphs and a supplied one-dimensional local chain. Norm conservation, covariance, and additive refinement permit different site measures. Repeated-value refinement closes exactly only when the measure-normalized external rates agree within each coarse block. When they do not, eliminating the complementary coordinates yields coherent memory and an initial-data forcing term, not stochastic noise or irreversible decoherence. A three-site example separates return to the coarse subspace at one time from autonomous coarse evolution. On a uniform pair-refined cycle, a contrast of vanishing norm retains finite energy feedback; a corrected nearest-neighbor generator has a fixed-band, finite-time second-order compressed estimate. Static elimination induces both stiffness and a generally nondiagonal metric. For uniformly positive nonuniform couplings, the normalized static graph has fourth-order low-energy eigenvalue accuracy, but its general prepared-state estimate is separately only first order. A contracting inverse series controls finite-range approximation, with additional costs for normalization and evolution. First-resolvent dressing improves an isolated low mode's state and phase ceiling to fourth order under quantitative spectral separation. The contribution is the source-bound combination of these conditional statements and obstructions, not a new general Schur, projection-memory, or subspace-perturbation mechanism. Geometry, measure, couplings, preparation, clock, action scale, and any empirical readout interpretation remain supplied.
tags: complementarity; graph refinement; coherent memory; induced metric; Schur reduction; low-energy preparation; resolvent dressing; partial Lean formalization.
title: Complementary Fine Structure, Memory, and Effective Coarse Dynamics

summary: Hardware-operable failures (HOFs) interrupt large language model (LLM) training but permit recovery on the same hardware without reset, repair, or replacement. Existing recovery systems nevertheless reload checkpoints, recompute lost progress, and rebuild process state, idling GPUs that could otherwise continue training. We present Leto, a fault-tolerant training system that leverages surviving hardware to enable efficient in-place recovery. Our key insight is that the state needed to resume training can be retained or prepared outside the active training process while remaining on the same hardware. Leto retains the working model state and the reusable process state, and preinitializes the remaining state in a shadow trainer. We devise two-tier erasure protection and chunk-level transactional updates to keep the retained model state recoverable and consistent, and reclaim the shadow state when active training needs its GPU memory. Evaluation on 6- and 72-GPU NVIDIA A100 clusters shows that Leto recovers 3.6--6.5$\times$ faster than the best-performing checkpointing baselines and improves productive training time by up to 13.7 percentage points. Large-scale simulation shows over 95% productive training time on a 131,072-GPU cluster.
title: Leto: Fast In-Place Recovery for LLM Training on Surviving Hardware

summary: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.
title: YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents

summary: Controlling an agent with vision requires being able to separate useful information from irrelevant background information. JEPA-style latent world models seem like a natural approach for this, as they do not perform pixel-level reconstruction; however, they are still sensitive to these distractor signals and experience latent collapse. In this work, we introduce Controllability Factorized JEPA (CF-JEPA), a JEPA-style world model which splits the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces. This factorization allows us to capture all the distractor information into the uncontrollable region, while we use the control-relevant latent information for our task. With this, we show comparable performance across 2D and 3D control tasks under nominal conditions and improved performance under distracted conditions, where CF-JEPA is the only model that does not experience latent collapse. We also validate our model under distracted conditions for a simulated robot task, highlighting the practical application of such a scheme.
title: CF-JEPA: Improving Robustness of JEPA World Models via Controllability Factorization

summary: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.
title: SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

summary: KV cache pruning reduces long-context inference memory usage by evicting less important key-value pairs. KVzip estimates importance through context reconstruction: prompting a model to repeat the context chunk by chunk. This achieves strong compression quality at the cost of additional forward passes. Learned approximations reduce this cost but require model-specific training. We analyze how KVzip identifies important cached information and show how to approximate its reconstruction scores using information already computed during prefill. These findings motivate EchoPress, a training-free method that approximates reconstruction attention using queries and keys from standard prefill. For each request, it reconstructs only the first chunk to calibrate importance scores for the remaining context. Experiments on LongBench and RULER with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that EchoPress matches KVzip in task accuracy across eviction ratios from 50% to 90%, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 1.7-19.6 and total prefill time by a factor of up to 2.9. Code is available at https://github.com/ljwljwljwljw/kvpress/tree/echo-press.
title: EchoPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Pruning via Virtual Context Reconstruction

summary: This archive accompanies “Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data” by Xin Gao. It contains cached benchmark and fresh-target prediction tables, finite-pair curation summaries, cross-repository comparison materials, figure source tables, frozen manifests, and reproduction code for the non-hosted analyses. Run `python3 tools/recalculate_public_limited_companion.py` after extraction. The standard-library checker reconstructs retained confusion counts, Matthews correlation coefficients, pairwise disagreement summaries, and repository disagreement tiers without network access. This is a cached-statistics reproduction, not an end-to-end replay of every raw data pipeline or a hosted-model rerun. The archive deliberately excludes hosted-model MAPK14 per-item and aggregate outputs, Figure 8 source material, and raw payload, CIF, and run files because accepted-account redistribution terms were not retrieved. This is a conservative packaging decision and does not claim that the excluded material is necessarily restricted. Software is MIT-licensed; ChEMBL-derived adaptations retain applicable CC BY-SA obligations. BindingDB source dumps and publisher PDFs are not included.
title: Public-limited companion materials for Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data

summary: Introduction.  In the early 2020s, the strategic presence of the Federal Republic of Germany in the Global South entered a phase of systemic crisis. In an attempt to reverse this trend, offi cial Berlin intensifi ed the use of political and military instruments in the Middle East, framing their deployment as a contribution to regional peace and stability. This article aims to assess the content and eff ectiveness of Germany's political and military measures, as well as their actual impact on confl ict resolution and the regional balance of power. Materials and Methods.  The empirical basis of the study draws on documents from the Office of the Federal Chancellor, the Bundestag, the Federal Foreign Office, and the Federal Ministry of Defence for the period 2006–2026. The research combines comparative analysis, event analysis, and discourse analysis, allowing for a systematic examination of the evolution of German foreign policy rhetoric, the dynamics of high-level official visits, and the patterns of Bundeswehr military presence in the region. Results.  Within the framework of the course toward “strategic restraint”, Germany formed a positive foreign policy image: in 2003, it refused to support the invasion of Iraq; subsequent efforts to strengthen its positions (including participation in security sector reform and the fi ght against ISIS) demonstrated limited effectiveness. On the Palestinian issue and the Lebanese settlement, Berlin declared its commitment to the “two states for two peoples” formula and to the territorial integrity of Lebanon. However, the unconditional priorities remained consideration of Israel's interests and the special nature of relations with it. After October 7, 2023, the FRG expressed political solidarity with Israel in its confrontation with Hamas and the Iran-backed “axis of resistance”. In 2025–2026, Berlin shifted to an open course of containing Iran. At the same time, Germany consistently avoided direct military involvement and took into account the positions of the Gulf monarchies. Conclusion.  Germany's demonstrated caution in the use of force served not so much as a manifestation of balance as a cover for its limited influence and piecemeal military presence in the region. The low effectiveness of the FRG's participation in conflict resolution is explained by a shift in goals. Berlin's main task is not conflict resolution, but the containment of actors rejecting the Western-centric model of world order. The article is addressed to specialists in the fi eld of international security and researchers of relations between the Global North and the Global South.
title: Germany's Policy in the Middle East Regarding Peace and Security: Achievements and Miscalculations

summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript “Cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye”. The package contains the analysis-ready modelling sample, Google Earth Engine and Python analysis scripts, locked out-of-fold model predictions, model-selection records, sensitivity-analysis outputs, uncertainty and calibration results, derived tables and figures, random seeds, data dictionaries, provenance information, and supporting quality-control documentation. The study evaluates the transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery across five 2021 wildfire complexes in southwestern Türkiye using outer leave-one-fire-out validation and spatially blocked inner cross-validation. The repository supports reproduction and auditing of the reported analyses. Source Sentinel-2, CORINE Land Cover, EFFIS, MODIS MCD64A1, and other third-party datasets remain subject to their original providers’ terms and licences. Spectral recovery reported in this study should not be interpreted as complete biomass, ecosystem, or restoration recovery.
title: Reproducibility package for cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye

summary: This repository supports research on single-channel speaker distance estimation : estimating the distance between a talker and a microphone from a single channel of reverberant speech. The record accompanies a series of papers investigating how reverberation, early and late room responses, and non-acoustic shortcut cues affect speaker-distance estimation. It combines a controlled synthetic corpus with real-corpus annotations and predefined evaluation splits. Source code and data-loading utilities are available at the project repository: https://github.com/michaelneri/audio-distance-estimation Dataset contents The record contains three main components: Synthetic RIR-variant corpus.  40,000 simulated speech clips arranged as 2,500 controlled acoustic scenes, with 16 paired variants per scene. Total size: approximately 25.9 GB. STARSS23 distance subset.  2,934 real speech clips extracted from STARSS23 and annotated with source–microphone distance. Total size: approximately 270 MB. Annotations and splits.  label tables, predefined folds, metadata, and reconstruction information for QMULTIMIT, VoiceHome-2, and the WHAM! noise conditions. These files contain no audio and are less than 2 MB. The downloadable archives are: synthetic_baseline.zip  10,000 clips with both propagation-delay and amplitude cues available. synthetic_gain_var.zip 10,000 clips with the amplitude cue disrupted by random ±6 dB source-gain variation. synthetic_onset_randomized.zip 10,000 clips with the propagation-delay cue disrupted by randomized onset padding. synthetic_both.zip 10,000 clips with both shortcut cues disrupted. shared_rir.zip 2,500 room impulse responses (RIRs) in .npz format, shared by all synthetic configurations. STARSS23_distance.zip 2,934 annotated real speech clips. labels_and_splits.zip   label tables, folds5.csv , and configuration metadata. MANIFEST.sha256 SHA-256 checksums for the downloadable archives. The four synthetic archives are independent and can be downloaded selectively. They all use the same RIR collection and synthetic fold assignment. Synthetic RIR-variant corpus The synthetic corpus is designed as a controlled experimental resource for isolating the contribution of different components of the room impulse response and two non-acoustic distance cues: propagation delay and received signal level. For each of 2,500 acoustic scenes , the dataset provides 16 paired signals . Room geometry, source and microphone positions, RIR, and speech segment are held fixed within a scene. Consequently, corresponding variants differ only in the specified experimental manipulation. RIR variants Each scene contains four acoustic variants: full — complete room impulse response. direct — direct path only, using a 2 ms window with a 5 ms half-cosine fade. no_early — direct path plus the late reverberant tail, with early reflections removed. no_late — direct path plus early reflections, with the late reverberant tail removed. The boundary between early and late reverberation is the room-specific mixing time , calculated from the mean free path rather than using a single fixed threshold. This allows the decomposition to follow the geometry of each simulated room. Shortcut-cue configurations Two cues can allow a model to estimate distance without relying on reverberation: propagation delay, represented by the signal onset timing; received level, determined by distance and source gain. Four configurations are provided: Configuration Timing cue Amplitude cue Manipulation baseline available available none gain_var available disrupted random ±6 dB source gain onset_randomized disrupted available randomized onset padding both disrupted disrupted both manipulations Onset randomization is applied to the convolved signal rather than the RIR. The random padding spans the natural propagation-delay range, while leaving the acoustic response itself unchanged. File structure and metadata Each sy

summary: Plate tectonics movements shape the surface of our Earth over geological time scales (millions to billions of years), and are responsible for the formation of mountains, oceanic basins and the shape of continents. The long-term dynamics of the Earth system, such as in the biogeochemical cycles or the constant evolution of geography/topography, are also known to be strongly controlled by tectonic activity. Using plate tectonic models, the Earth’s past geography can be reconstructed into palaeo Digital Elevation Models (palaeo-DEMs) that account for past sea-level changes and depict changes in ocean-continents distribution. Users of these products, such as climate modellers interested in understanding the Earth’s past climates, require metrics and analytical solutions to describe the palaeo-DEMs and the changes from one reconstruction to the next. While relatively straightforward to compute static indicators for one single map and plot evolutions over time (e.g., of global oceanic area or high altitudes regions), understanding and representing transitions within and between states (e.g., land and water) has not yet addressed in palaeogeography. With this case study, we present an application of the Living Earth framework to deep-time palaeogeographic maps, focusing on 45 time steps spanning the Phanerozoic era (last 545 million years), as a complement to existing static geographic indicators.
title: Presentation: Living Earth for Deep-time: Understanding the Earth's Evolving Geography and Climate for the Last 545 Million Years

summary: Figure 1. Conceptual framework linking production, market access and household welfare. Figure 1 summarises the study’s conceptual transmission mechanism. Farm production and resource exposure influence market access and travel costs, which subsequently affect prices, wages, labour allocation and household consumption welfare. The integration channel operates through stronger competition, lower transaction costs and improved conversion of production into consumption. The pressure channel captures the possibility that local price increases, labour reallocation, congestion and unequal bargaining power may weaken or redistribute the welfare gains from improved connectivity. Figure 2. Marginal association of log production with log consumption across market access and resource dependence. Figure 2 plots the marginal association between agricultural production and household consumption over the observed market-access range at low, median and high levels of resource dependence. The three lines slope upward, indicating that better market access strengthens the conversion of production into consumption welfare. The slope is steepest under low resource dependence and weakest under high resource dependence, showing that resource dependence attenuates, but does not reverse, the production-access welfare premium. The shaded bands represent 95% confidence intervals. Figure 3. Country-specific production-by-market-access estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Figure 3 compares the production-by-market-access coefficient across Ghana, Mozambique, Nigeria, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia. Every point estimate is positive, and every 95% confidence interval lies above zero, indicating a consistently positive production-access complementarity across the six countries. The estimated association is strongest in Mozambique and Tanzania and smallest in Nigeria and Ghana. The wider interval for Mozambique reflects lower statistical precision associated with its smaller national sample. Sources of data The empirical dataset combines harmonised household-survey observations with spatial-accessibility, geological, climatic, nighttime-lights, price and labour-market information. The complete analytical file contains 68,000 household observations from Ghana, Mozambique, Nigeria, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia. Country survey names, waves, panel structures, observation counts and regional coverage are documented in the Survey_Metadata worksheet of the replication workbook.
title: Market Access and Rural Welfare: Production Transmission, Resource Dependence and Spatial Spillovers in Six African Economies

summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.
title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

summary: This dataset was produced using a harmonised methodology for estimating the spatial distribution of citrus areas across the European Union at 10 × 10 km grid resolution for the 2020 reference year. The approach integrates Eurostat **Farm Structure Survey (FSS) 2020** gridded agricultural statistics, official regional agricultural statistics and the Copernicus High Resolution Layer (HRL) Crop Types. Missing or suppressed FSS values are estimated using regional crop-area totals and Earth Observation-derived spatial weights, while reported values are transferred, aggregated or disaggregated to the common EEA reference grid according to their source resolution. The resulting map provides quantitative citrus-area estimates, crop-presence indicators, provenance metadata and a rule-based methodological uncertainty class for each grid cell. Evaluation against official regional statistics and independent **Land Use/Cover Area Frame Survey (LUCAS)** field observations showed overall consistency with the source statistics and a 95.1% detection rate for LUCAS-positive grid cells. The resulting spatial dataset is intended to support EFSA plant health risk assessment and related spatial analyses.
title: Spatial distribution of citrus areas in the European Union at 10 × 10 km grid resolution, 2020

summary: Scroll Score for Shift/Work ISSOTL17 Poster Presentation, Calgary, Canada Shift/Workshops are composed and disseminated by being performed. Playing the score leads to it being re-calibrated for future performances. Speculations was commissioned by the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, India. It was first performed at Edinburgh Sculpture Workshop (3-4 March 2017). At ESW, three ‘branch’ scores were composed to be performed in Kochi (22-23 March 2017) and at the Kristiansand Theatre, University of Agder, Norway (28-20 Aug 2017) producing further branch scores. A SoTL analysis of Speculations was presented at ISSoTL17 in Calgary, October 2017. Recalibrated through intense peer-review, a ‘Scroll Score’ of the generative composition to date was published as an open educational resource (OER) for ISSoTL17 (12 & 14 Oct 2017) and published on shift-work.org.ukShift/Work: Speculations is an innovative methodology that synthesises practice-based and practice-led research methods to transform our understanding and knowledge of artistic research (AR). It develops powerful insights into how Peer-2-Peer methods transmute speculative artistic practices by coupling the taking of risks with experiencing their consequences. Speculations combines new theories of paragogy with SoTL (Scholarship of Teaching & Learning) and Participatory Action Research (PAR) methods to develop and enhance a metacognitive understanding of AR. Through this, it invents a new theoretical framework - the ‘paratechnic’ - a means to collectively ‘score’ and disseminate artistic research as an OER. This is of particular importance to widening participation in the arts and restoring their civic purpose.‘Speculation’ is a unifying ethics (or cognitive bias) in AR commonly expressed as ‘without a script’ or ‘not knowing’. Drawing explicit attention to an implicit ethics within AR, and exposing it to the scrutiny and practices of non-artistic learners, raises awareness of its operations and limitations. This, in turn, enables us to repurpose, invent and practice metacognitive forms of speculation that have operational significance for, and beyond, AR.Speculations (Punctum) and newmaterialism.eu have been pivotal in suggesting ludic and non-anthropocentric forms of emergence that might foreground, and move beyond, AR's cognitive biases. Generative Shift/Work composition activates material probes as autopoetic catalysts for problem creation. As component interactions made radically distinct objects from the same material, speculation enabled Shift/Workers to formulate the concepts, equipment, and techniques to generate the truly collaborative ability to fabricate common research objects.Originality:Speculations is an original contribution to artistic knowledge, art andragogy and artistic research that implements emerging methods in paragogy and pioneers SoTL in art. A theoretically reflexive, participatory, and openly accessible paragogy for artistic research, Speculations liberates artistic knowledges by common-ing the proprietary ‘secret skills’ of the guild-monotechnic.Significance:Speculations has broad political, ontological and epistemological significance. Establishing a collective ontology for art practice though paragogy, Speculations exemplifies collectivist whole-systems thinking. Speculative research methods recognise that art is a subsystem of society - rather than separate from it - and ensure it has a pragmatic sense of its transformative potential.Rigour:Speculations is a scholarly, coherent, iterative system of meta-cognitive peer review. Composition is scaffolded with an academic and artistic community of ‘Shift/Workers’. Shift/Workers compose and play-test each other’s workshop scores before calibrating them through collective peer-review. Scores are then re-performed, iteratively, at international peer-reviewed artistic and scholarly events.
title: Unlearning Scroll Score

summary: We report the developments obtained after PIHR–GOLDBACH XIX (Gold-19) in the continuing attempt to isolate a rigorous analytic route toward the binary Goldbach conjecture. Gold-19 returned from the endpoint Möbius-variance formulation of Gold-18 to the signed determinant geometry of Gold-17. Its central candidate theorem, Endpoint Coefficient-Preserving Kloosterman Transfer (ECPKT), asked that the parity-sensitive four-weight determinant block be converted, without destructive absolute-value majorization, into bilinear Kloosterman forms with two -controlled coefficient vectors. The post-Gold-19 analysis substantially sharpens that proposal. First, a false shortcut has been eliminated. The centered endpoint large-sieve/Ramaré block does not itself contain the reciprocal geometry required by the strongest Kloosterman estimates. Opening the square produces Ramanujan sums rather than Kloosterman sums, so the modular inverse must already come from the underlying determinant or congruence geometry. Second, the algebraic core of ECPKT can be carried out explicitly. If the character diagonalization of Gold-17 is stopped one Gauss transformation earlier, a two-weight arithmetic block admits an exact Partial-Gauss Kloosterman Transfer
title: Localized Partial-Gauss Transfer, Semiprime Kloosterman Coverage, and the Remaining Structured-Sieve Ledger in the Binary Goldbach Problem (PIHR-Goldach-XX) Progress Beyond PIHR–GOLDBACH XIX: From Endpoint Coefficient-Preserving Transfer to a Localized Partial-Gauss Closure Candidate

summary: We present a complete, self-contained analysis of the one-loop functional renormalization group (FRG) flow of Quantum Distortion Gravity (QDG), a metric-affine framework with gauged Weyl symmetry. We derive the classical foundations from first principles: the irreducible decomposition of the distortion tensor with an explicit inversion of the trace matrix, the Weyl-covariant distortion $\tilde D$, the no-go theorem for bare distortion invariants, and the Weyl-invariant ultraviolet action with distortion entering through $\phi^2 I_i[\tilde D]$. We then establish the constraint structure of the truncated theory (8 physical degrees of freedom, no spin-2 ghost) via a complete Dirac--Bergmann analysis, and analyze the BRST--BV quantization of the gauge algebra $Diff(\mathcal M) \ltimes Weyl$, including the antifield spectrum, the nilpotency proof, and the classical master equation. We compute the Weyl anomaly coefficients from heat-kernel data and prove the anomaly is cancellable by a Wess--Zumino term. In the main part of the paper we derive all one-loop beta functions from first principles, keeping every intermediate step. We show that in unitary gauge, the dilaton is a gauge mode and does not contribute; Proca fields contribute with three transverse polarizations and no Faddeev--Popov ghosts; Dirac fermions contribute via the Litim fermionic regulator. We extract the matter coefficients $a_S = +1/2$, $a_D = -2$, and $a_V = +3/2$ (the last for a Proca vector in unitary gauge), and we verify each by two independent routes. We derive the gravitational anomalous dimension from the explicit trace over TT graviton, trace mode, and Faddeev--Popov ghosts, reproducing the Litim result $A(\lambda)$ and $B(\lambda)$, and we display the ADM decomposition that yields the mode multiplicities. We show that the fixed-point equation $\beta_{\tilde G} = 0$ is genuinely quadratic in $\tilde G$ at fixed $\lambda$, we solve it explicitly, and we give the resulting discriminant. For the Standard Model matter content ($n_f = 3$, $n_V = 2$), we find a non-trivial UV fixed point at $\tilde G^* \approx 0.43$, $\lambda^* \approx -0.02$, with two relevant directions in the $(\tilde G, \lambda)$ sector, and we compute the stability matrix, critical exponents, and their numerical uncertainties. We verify robustness with a sensitivity scan, showing the fixed point exists for all $C_{\rm bl} > C_{\rm bl}^{\rm crit} \approx -1.02$, well above the QDG value $C_{\rm bl} = -3/(2\pi) \approx -0.477$; we give the analytic form of the critical line. We also analyze the heat kernel in a background field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$, showing that the mixing between graviton and Proca in the $(h^{01}, V^1)$ sector gives a negative contribution to the FRG coefficient $\hat c_V$ (distinct from the Weyl-anomaly coefficient $c^{\rm W}$), and we exhibit the second-order heat-kernel trace explicitly. Finally, we discuss scale generation via Coleman--Weinberg in a two-scalar extension, derive the flat-direction condition, and compare our results with the recent Proca--gravity fixed point of Pastor-Marcos et al. All symbolic and numerical calculations are performed in Python (SymPy, NumPy, SciPy), and the complete code is provided in the appendices, together with additional verification scripts.
title: Quantum Distortion Gravity: A Complete One-Loop Analysis of the Minimal Truncation

summary: Data and Python code accompanying the manuscript “Replication-Based Criteria Can Change the Selected Number of Clusters: A Seven-Criterion Audit of k-Means on Indonesian Provincial Environmental Data” (submitted to the Journal of Computing Theories and Applications). The package audits how the number of clusters, k, is selected for k-means on a small tabular dataset: the published components of Indonesia’s Environmental Quality Index (Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup) for 38 provinces, 2021–2024. Seven criteria are computed for k = 2 to 8: the within-cluster sum of squares (read visually and by two formal knee rules), silhouette width, the Davies–Bouldin and Calinski–Harabasz indices, the gap statistic, subsample stability (adjusted Rand index over 200 pairs of overlapping 80% subsamples) and agreement with Ward linkage. The scripts also run sensitivity analyses, a comparison of six clustering algorithms, fixed-centroid assignment across years, a leave-one-out comparison of regression models for the air quality component, permutation importance and exact Shapley values. Contents: data/ (index components 2021–2024; GRDP per capita and population density; a cell-level provenance audit), code/ (six analysis scripts and a plotting-style module), README.md (run order, variable dictionary and data sources), requirements.txt (pinned library versions), CITATION.cff and licence files. Running the six scripts in the order given in README.md reproduces every table and figure of the manuscript in about four minutes on a laptop (Python 3.11 or later). The indicator values are official statistics from Statistics Indonesia (Badan Pusat Statistik) and are reproduced unchanged. Please cite the original BPS tables as well as this record. Code: MIT licence. Data files: CC BY 4.0.
tags: k-means; number of clusters; cluster validation; clustering stability; adjusted Rand index; environmental quality index; Indonesia; reproducibility

summary: This release contains the research artifacts for “Trustworthy Evaluation Frameworks for AI-Assisted Painting Restoration,” a master’s thesis at the University of Applied Sciences Technikum Wien. The study develops and applies an evidence-based evaluation framework combining traditional image quality metrics with perceptual, colour, texture, boundary, structural, robustness, and generative-uncertainty evidence. The Controlled-300 study covers 300 paintings across five categories, with 3,425 registered cases and 2,620 eligible cases. Four methods: OpenCV Telea, LaMa, HINT, and Stable Diffusion, provide 10,480 matched primary candidates. The broader reporting collection contains 13,879 retained candidates. Additional investigations include 1,025 four-seed Stable Diffusion uncertainty groups, damage-size sensitivity, mask robustness, synthetic degradation, and separate diagnostic studies. SDXL is included as a bounded feasibility investigation, not as a fifth full-coverage method. Across 2,320 matched non-zero-damage cases, LaMa achieved the best mean masked MAE (14.83) and crop LPIPS (0.1292), while Telea achieved the best mean crop SSIM (0.8632). These complementary results motivate examining restoration quality through multiple forms of saved evidence. The archive brings together source code, notebooks, configurations, painting provenance, experimental outputs, candidate restorations, diagnostic maps, metric tables, reports, and supporting documentation. An accompanying eight room Streamlit dashboard presents the saved findings interactively. Release manifests and checksums document the archived files. Model weights and execution environments are not included. Licensing and third-party exclusions are described in the accompanying rights notice. Download and extraction: The research archive is distributed as eight numbered parts ( .zip.001 to .zip.008 ). Download all eight parts and follow REASSEMBLE.txt to reconstruct and verify the original ZIP before extraction. The parts are not independently extractable archives. SPLIT_MANIFEST.json records each part’s size and checksums; SHA256SUMS.txt covers the uploaded files. Splitting changes only the delivery format: the research contents remain unchanged.   Source code and documentation Interactive research dashboard Candidate restoration repository Diagnostics repository
title: Trustworthy Evaluation Frameworks for AI-Assisted Painting Restoration: Controlled-300 Research Artifacts

summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.
title: The Inverse Berggren Tree Problem

summary: This paper proposes a modified special–relativistic framework in which rest energy is carried by the temporal component of the Minkowski metric through a scalar ζ= e −φ , realized as a dilaton that couples to matter through the temporal leg of the metric alone. A particle is postulated to convert—by a graviton–mediated process with cycle energy E= A/f—between a massive (ζ →0) and a massless (ζ = 1) state, reaching the light–speed limit without the usual infinite–energy obstruction. Part I develops the framework: the temporal mass term, the conversion oscillation, graviton kinematics derived from four–momentum conservation, a covariant (disformal, preferred–frame) action for the temporal dilaton, and a modified Einstein equation that covariant conservation forces back to general relativity. Part II, more speculatively, identifies ζ 2 with the inverse of the temporal element G int of the pentadimensional Deformed Space–Time (DST) metrics of gravity and the strong interaction (ζ 2 = 1/G int ; the electroweak metrics are read as the luminal ζ = 1 branch), used strictly as a phenomenological parametrization; extends the geometry to a Calabi–Yau threefold (the T 6 /Z 3 orbifold worked out explicitly; three generations require discrete Wilson lines on it or a different manifold); and proposes a dictionary between Standard–Model particles, features of that manifold, and a tetrahedral nuclear model, resting on numerical correspondences rather than derivations. Confrontation with data is stated as four survival conditions (S1–S4): the temporal scalar must be short–ranged (m φ ≳5 meV); planetary ephemerides bound the conversion constant, f esc A≲5 ×10 −31 W per nucleon (f esc the radiated fraction of a cycle); ordinary matter cannot feed the dark sector at cosmological rates; and the dark–sector conjecture survives only as a dark–sector–internal exchange tied to an evolving w(z). The one laboratory target is an α ≈ 2 Yukawa correction to gravity at λ ≈ 4–10 µm with no equivalence–principle violation. A closing section reads the author’s movie of cellular convection on the surface of hot water as a kinematic analogue of the cosmic web (an Analogy, not evidence), gives the dark–sector exchange its interacting–dark–energy form, and adds a fifth survival condition (S5: any variation of Gconfined to the dark sector) and a survey target (T2); the analogy itself is evidence for none of these.

summary: Abstract: Efficient sensing remains critical in low-cost Internet of Things (IoT) and Web of Things (WoT)-enabled edge nodes, even when the sensor itself is inexpensive and widely used. The DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor employs a single-wire dig-ital protocol and relies on Arduino libraries for data acquisition, timeout handling, and scheduling behavior. In this paper, eight Arduino DHT11 libraries are benchmarked on an Arduino Uno R3 using six criteria: flash memory usage, SRAM consumption, average measured call duration, timing variability, maximum CPU blocking time, and failure-recovery behavior. The results reveal substantial performance trade-offs. Aver-age measured call durations ranged from 5,588 µs for the asynchronous DHT Sensors Non-Blocking implementation to approximately 1.04 s for DHT11; however, these measurements reflect different execution semantics and should not be interpreted as directly equivalent end-to-end acquisition latencies. Flash usage ranged from 4,288 to 5,244 bytes, while SRAM consumption ranged from 238 to 266 bytes. TroykaDHT and SDHT delivered the most stable low-latency readings, DFRobot_DHT11 minimized SRAM usage, and DHT Sensors Non-Blocking was most suitable when asynchronous execution and reduced continuous CPU occupation were required. This study does not directly benchmark application-layer protocols or cloud services, such as HTTP, MQTT, REST, or WebSocket; instead, it characterizes sensing-layer behavior that can influence data freshness, task scheduling, and overall responsiveness in resource-constrained IoT/WoT edge deployments.
title: Performance Analysis of Arduino DHT11 Sensor Libraries for Resource-constrained IoT/WoT Edge Nodes.

summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.
title: Data and code for "Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change"

summary: The laws of physics are CPT-symmetric, yet laboratory quantum mechanics prepares the past and only samples the future. This working paper distinguishes five levels of taking the symmetry seriously — symmetric laws with the open future left implicit, a two-boundary description, symmetric processes, a nontrivial final boundary, and laboratory access to it — places published views and experiments on them, and states what each predicts for a final-boundary test, in which an engineered terminal acts on a flag and an entangled partner is read on every trial. Exact results: an open future propagates backward through any physical channel; a terminal can only transfer, never manufacture, final-side contrast, giving lambda = tanh(hbar omega / 2 k T_f) in a swap model, the mirror of a reset; a clamp of budget A needs an energy of at least k T_f ln A in some branch; under free local control any every-trial final condition signals, with visibility equal to the clamp strength. Under stated transfer models a null reads as a lower bound on a swap-equivalent final temperature (Partridge: above 3.5e7 K for escaping microwaves; planned qubit tests: about 27 K and 360 K). The paper audits transport to the future, specifies what any physical source of a final condition must supply, and finds that no named candidate meets the specification. CPT motivates the reversed-resource question; channel duality bounds its possible transfer; laboratory access remains an additional physical hypothesis, decided only by experiment. No new experimental result is reported. Drafted with AI assistance and revised after AI-assisted reviews; responsibility rests with the author.
tags: CPT symmetry; arrow of time; two-boundary quantum mechanics, final boundary condition; absorber theory; Landauer principle; postselection; no-signalling; two-way quantum computing
title: How seriously do we take CPT? Levels of time-symmetry acceptance, and what each predicts for final-boundary tests and two-way quantum computing

summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

summary: Dependency parsers often receive morphological features as part of their input, but the source and completeness of those features are rarely treated as experimental variables. We study German Case in a controlled setting by comparing dependency parsers trained with no Case, independently predicted Case, and gold Case. Using pinned German-GSD and German-HDT Universal Dependencies resources, we audit Case coverage and provenance, construct matched feature conditions, and evaluate both in-domain parsing and cross-treebank transfer. In a three-seed, 1,000-step T4 pilot, predicted Case has higher mean labeled attachment than no Case and higher overall mean LAS than gold Case under HDT transfer for all three seeds. The difference is concentrated on tokens where gold Case is missing; on gold-Case-present tokens, predicted Case is 0.47 LAS points below gold Case on average. Sentence-level paired bootstrap intervals for the aggregate HDT comparison exclude zero, while the in-domain predicted-versus-gold comparison remains seed-sensitive. We use these results to study feature source and annotation completeness while treating the parser and training setup as a controlled feasibility study.
title: Feature Source and Annotation Completeness in German Dependency Parsing

summary: Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM) describes the photon as an energetic physical entity whose interaction with an external gravitational field proceeds by direct force- and energy–momentum exchange, rather than through the geometric curvature of spacetime. This paper develops the ECM account of photon dynamics in external gravitational fields, with gravitational redshift interpreted as the expenditure of an acquired gravitational interaction-energy component Eɢ rather than as a depletion of the photon’s inherent frequency-defined energy. The photon’s inherent state is fixed by Eᵢₙₕₑᵣₑₙₜ = hf_photon = −Mᵃᵖᵖc², where Mᵃᵖᵖ < 0 is the Negative Apparent Mass (NAM) associated with the energetic reduction of the emitting electron. A coordinate framework for the photon–field interaction is constructed in which successive interaction stages generate external-field momentum displacements through Δpₑₓₜ = h/Δλ and its reverse-branch counterpart Δpₑₓₜ = h/(−Δλ), organised as a symmetric blueshift–redshift trajectory about the inherent reference state. The complete state-generation chain x° → f → Δf → λ → Δλ → Δpₑₓₜ → ΔG is established together with the ECM phase transformation Tₓˆ = x°/360°f = Δt, providing a rigorous, data-driven basis for graphing the exchange without arbitrary coordinates. An explicit nine-point displacement data set is specified, the complete coordinate table is computed, and the exchange trajectory is graphed.
title: Photon Dynamics in External Gravitational Fields: Energy–Momentum Exchange Between Photons and Gravitational Fields in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. Asimismo, incorpora procedimientos para auditoría me

summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. When a high-confidence correction is found, GradLint can emit repaired FSL and/or MRtrix gradient files together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs.  The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. This record archives the source code for GradLint v1.1.6, corresponding to the GitHub release published on 2026-10-03. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. summary: Language functions not only as a means of transmitting information but also as a repository of cultural knowledge, collective experience, and culturally shaped patterns of thought. Consequently, translation involves more than the transfer of lexical and grammatical information between languages. It also requires the interpretation and reconstruction of meanings that are embedded within particular cultural contexts. This issue becomes especially evident in the translation of idioms, proverbs, metaphors, realia, and other culture-specific expressions whose meanings cannot always be derived from their individual lexical components. In Translation Studies, such elements are commonly discussed as culture-specific items (CSIs), which may require particular strategies to preserve their semantic, pragmatic, and cultural dimensions in the target language (Aixelá, 1996).
tags: Idiomatic expressions provide a particularly clear illustration of the relationship between language and culture.

summary: Classical metaphysics treats the mutual exclusivity of alternatives as primitive: or, in its physical reading, excludes by nature. This paper argues the polarity should be reversed. Exclusivity is an achievement — stated, interior, structural content of the alternatives them-selves — rather than an intrinsic feature of disjunction; and once exclusion is relocated from the exterior of or to interior content, a new composition regime falls out with no further postulation: the joint regime, in which co-present alternatives simply decline to carry mu-tual negations. The difference between the regimes is fixed by a one-statement test, which answers the suspicion of mere notation; a strict fence separates what the new primitive sup-plies (openness) from anything its occupants might do with it (use), which blocks the two natural misreadings; and the primitive itself receives a deflationary definition: or-jointness is the logic-valued regime of not stating mutual negations on the interior side — obtained by declension, not addition. We argue the proposal reclassifies the color-exclusion problem that fractured the Tractatus, and supplies the determinable-based literature on metaphysical indeterminacy with the composition story it has lacked. A documented fact about the direction of discovery then bears on the proposal’s status: the two composition forms were first extracted, in companion work, from the case-by-case structure of interference phenomena — before the present philosophy existed — so the dichotomy’s shape is explained by what it was extracted from, not by any philosophical purpose it might serve. Whether the world instantiates the joint regime is the companion framework’s proposal, on which no thesis here leans; what the provenance establishes is that the primitive was not gerrymandered for the argument that now exposes it.
title: Exclusivity as Achievement: Relocating Mutual Exclusion to the Interior, and the Logical Primitive That Falls Out

summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . Keywords: Abstract algebra, cyclic groups, direct products, exponent coordinates, re- lation lattices, projection functors, natural transformations, Newton identities, Chinese Remainder Theorem, rank complexity. summary: This dataset supports the study “A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection.” It contains accession-level manifests, derived statistical tables, figure-source data, documentation, software-version information, and analysis code supporting an assembly-first workflow with raw-read reconstruction for publicly available sequencing records. Starting from 44,278 geographically resolved eligible records, 1,687 records had no analyzable public genome input, leaving 42,591 records with an analyzable genome input. Of these, two were excluded during final cohort harmonization, resulting in a final analytical collection of 42,589 K. pneumoniae genomes. This collection comprised 40,093 genomes represented by usable public assemblies and 2,496 genomes reconstructed from publicly available sequencing reads. The deposit does not redistribute genome assemblies or raw sequencing reads. Sequence data should be retrieved from the relevant public repositories using the accession identifiers provided in the manifests. The archived materials support reproduction of the post-assembly cohort audit, statistical summaries, and figures. The exact raw-read preprocessing commands used for the rescued genomes were not retained; consequently, adapter-trimming and quality-filtering parameters are not represented as reproducible components of this deposit. Reconstructed and deposited assemblies were nevertheless evaluated using the same post-assembly quality-control criteria before inclusion in the final analytical collection. Jianhua Li and Jing Guo contributed equally to this work. Jing Chen is the corresponding author. Correspondence: dongqingfei@126.com . summary: The P versus NP problem has resisted every method, and three theorems explain why: relativization, natural proofs and algebrization each prove that a whole family of arguments cannot separate the classes. We derive P ≠ NP from existence by a machine-checked chain in which every step but one is a theorem. An arrow exists as a theorem with no premise; the problem's native involution, complementation, is proved to have no fixed point; and an absolute asymmetry is proved: what a registration destroys no procedure of any cost recovers, while what a search hides exhaustive search always recovers. A single identification, the bridge, equates this asymmetry with the separation, and on it P ≠ NP holds. We prove that the bridge is not a tautology and that it is equivalent to the separation, so the chain locates the entire content of the P versus NP problem in one explicit statement: every proof of P ≠ NP, by any method, is a proof of the bridge. A record theorem follows: the absence of a fixed locus, the exhaustiveness of black-box search, the thermodynamic price of computation with every step granted irreversible, and the destroyed-hidden asymmetry are true in a world where the classes are equal as in one where they differ, and so decide nothing; the structural and physical routes the paper names are closed by one theorem. All forty-nine theorems, in three kernels, are compiled in Lean 4.19.0 with no import, no custom axiom and no unproved step, and are printed in full. The reduction is complete in two registers: the form is closed at theorem grade, and the value, P ≠ NP, is closed on the bridge at premise grade, with machine-checked proof that no weaker premise replaces the bridge.
title: P versus NP Closed on One Posit: The Seat Proved Empty and the Separation Reduced by Machine to a Single Irreducible Bridge
